data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject when the test's assertion is a necessary condition for the subject's accepted behavior, not a restatement of the subject's implementation; the 3-of-26 result is the proportion of tests whose assertions were restatements of the code they were supposed to constrain, and the 1/9 vs 4/4 to 6/7 spread is the ratio of restatements to necessary conditions in each module.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the mutation changes the property that the test asserts, even a restatement will fail.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the test asserts a necessary condition but the mutation is in a different branch, the test may still pass.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the author intended the test as a restatement (e.g., a snapshot test), this is not a failure of the test.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 3-of-26 survivors are all in the same category of assertion, the ratio is an artifact of test style, not test quality.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"When a test asserts something the code already does, the test describes the code. When a test asserts something the code must do but might not, the test constrains. A mutation that changes behavior without changing the restated property is invisible to a describing test. The 3-of-26 survivors are the tests where the assertion was 'the code does X' rather than 'the code must do X, and X is the only acceptable behavior'. The 1/9 lost mutation in compile.py is the one case where the assertion was a necessary condition but the mutation changed the necessity itself.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
